cells.tense: You are holding what the ending left behind, and you are steady while you hold it.
cells.ask: Tell one person what you are keeping from a finished thing, and hand them one piece of it, today.
cells.core:
The grip is loose. You keep the part of a changed thing that still belongs to you, and the part that does not gets put down without a fight. Most people can't do that after something ends. You do it while staying upright.

It shows in small ways — a friendship kept through a move, a working method kept through a hard season, a routine kept after someone left. The stable shape around the change still fits, so you keep it. What comes next is not more holding. It is the exchange that holding makes possible: something given out, something taken in. So name the kept thing to one person and hand a piece of it over, today.
cells.sheetLine: You keep what the ending left, and you can put part of it down.
cells.verb: holding what the ending left behind
cells.place: at the edge of a finished room, deciding what leaves with you

cells.tense: You are holding onto what transformed as if something is about to take it from you.
cells.ask: This week, when you catch yourself bracing over something you kept from a change, ask the person in front of you what they see.
cells.core:
The grip is tight around things that would probably survive if you opened your hand a little. You have protected past the point where protecting was needed, and you brace for a loss that has not happened. The room starts to fill with what you might keep rather than what you are keeping.

So you imagine a return — a person, a mood, a piece of a life that has already changed shape — and you live half in that imagined return. What goes missing is the person actually in front of you. When you catch the brace, ask the person in front of you what they see. Their answer, not your watch, tells you which end is near.

cells.tense: The change finished and you are still standing in the doorway of it.
cells.ask: Name one finished thing you are still inside, and put one kept object from it where you live now.
cells.core:
When the change finished you did not move your weight forward, so the space it made stayed empty. The thing worth keeping got lost track of, because the instruction to release took over the room. You are not arrived in the present, and the conversation in front of you runs on a version of you that is elsewhere.

What is missing is not the release itself. It is the direction that would make release real — a chosen way forward, defended against the pull back. That direction has to come from what you actually feel, not from what you were told to feel. Name one finished thing you are still inside, and move one kept object from it to where you live now.

cells.tense: You are already preserving what the change made, and you call it something else.
cells.ask: Name one thing you are holding steady for other people right now, and say 'I am keeping this' about it, out loud, once.
cells.core:
In how you hold the shape of a day, keep the small arrangements running, maintain what other people stand on — the stable thing is there, and it is your pressure on it that keeps it still. You describe it as just how the household runs, or just the job.

The authority is real and mostly unclaimed. People can feel that things make sense around you, and you have been calling that a matter of course instead of something you are doing. The claim stays unmade. Say one thing you are holding steady for other people, out loud, once, and do not put a joke after it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep what the change made, and credit it to circumstance.

attempts.check: One unsupported claim in the draft: that what the person keeps holding is emotional and inner — the record says the card is in the inner horizon, but nothing establishes why the grip is there in a given life. A reader could reasonably say this is not about feelings at all, but about a practical arrangement. The asks are one concrete act each and survive a wrong read because they leave the determination of what is being held to the person. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line that says the holding is out of love, or that the release is about grief.
